activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Natalie wanted to paint a green frog at daycare. But she looked and looked. There was no green paint. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. No green.

Natalie was playing doctor with Sam before snack. She made Sam's teddy bear all better. Then she came back to the paint. She still wanted her frog. She asked, "Where can green come from?" The sun did not shine through the window. It was a rainy day. So the paints were all hers to try.

She put yellow paint on her brush. She added blue paint. She mixed it with her stick. It made a big messy blob. The blob turned green! "Yellow and blue make green!" said Natalie. She painted a big green frog. Then she painted one for Sam's teddy bear, too. The teddy bear doctor now had a frog.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Jack stood at the big window. He counted the planes. "One plane, two planes, three," he said. "Grandpa is on plane three." Grandma held his hand. Plane three landed. The door opened. Out came Grandpa with one big suitcase. "Grandpa!" Jack yelled. Grandpa hugged him soft and long.

At home, Grandpa opened the big suitcase. "I will stay for a whole week," he said. He put his shirts in the drawer. He put his socks in the drawer too. Jack watched. "Why do the clothes go in the drawer?" he asked. "A week is a long time," said Grandpa. "The drawer is my little home now."

Jack saw a small ant on the floor. "Look, Grandpa!" he said. "I like ants," said Grandpa. "I will watch it with you." They sat down together. Jack counted the ant's little legs. "One, two, three, four, five, six," he said. Grandpa smiled. Jack was young, and the week was just beginning. Grandpa said, "Now show me your toys."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Wesley went to the pet store with his dad. He saw a tall cage with a little brown rabbit inside. "I want that one," said Wesley. Dad smiled and said yes.

At home, Wesley put the rabbit in his new cage. But the rabbit hid in the corner. Wesley clapped his hands. "Come out!" he called. The rabbit hid deeper. Wesley felt a big worry in his tummy. "Dad, he doesn't like me."

"Let's be very quiet," said Dad. "New pets need calm." So they sat still. The room got quiet. Then the rabbit hopped out. It found a carrot and began to eat.

Wesley whispered, "He came out because we got quiet." The rabbit ate the carrot in a big circle. Wesley giggled softly. Dad put an arm around him. The rabbit hopped near Wesley's hand, warm and soft, and stayed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Mateo went to the library with his mama. He wanted to find a book all by himself. But he could not read the letters yet.

A girl sat at a small table. She patted the chair next to her. "Come look," she said. She opened a thick book full of letters.

"B is for bear," the girl said. "B says buh. Bear starts with buh." Mateo looked at the big letter B. He said, "Buh, buh, bear." He said it again, slow. "Buh."

Then he stood up. He walked past the shelves. He looked at book after book. He saw a B on a red cover. "Buh," he said. "Bear book?" He opened it. Yes! It was about bears.

"I found it because B says buh," Mateo told the girl. She smiled and patted the page. "Read it with me," she said.

Mateo sat down, nice and slow. He put his hand flat on the B. "Buh, buh, bear," he said, one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Violet went to the library with Grandma. She wanted a book about a red boat. She looked on the shelf where boats might hide.

The librarian gave her a card. "You can take books home," the librarian said. Violet picked a book with a boat on the front. The front cover had words on it. Grandma read them out loud. "Sail Away, Little Boat," Grandma said. "The words tell us the name!"

Violet opened the book. She turned the pages one by one. First the front, then the middle, then the back. Each page had more words. Grandma pointed at them. "These words say what the boat does," Grandma said. Violet touched the letters with her finger. The boat in the picture sailed on blue water.

At home, Violet read the book every night. She wanted to keep it forever. "Can this book stay with me always?" she asked. Grandma shook her head gently. "It has to go back. Other kids want to read it too." Violet felt a little sad. Grandma hugged her. "We can borrow it again another day."

On return day, Violet held the book tight. Then she put it in the return box. The book slid down with a soft thump. The librarian smiled. "Now another child can read about the boat," she said. Violet stood tall. "Because I gave it back!" she said. Grandma took her hand. "Let's pick a new book," said Grandma. Violet ran to the shelf.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Wesley came to school early. The room was quiet. Then his nose wiggled. Something smelled sweet. Wesley wanted to know what it was.

He looked with his eyes. He saw blocks and wood trucks. No cookies anywhere. He listened with his ears. He heard a little hum. It came from the kitchen. Wesley ran to Miss Jo. "Can my nose find the cookies?" he asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Yes. Your nose smells them. Let's walk." They walked and the smell got bigger. The hum got bigger too.

Miss Jo opened the oven door. Cookies! The hum was the oven, because the oven was hot. "The oven made them," Wesley said. He touched one cookie. It was warm on his fingers. He took a bite. Sweet on his tongue! "I found them with my nose!" he shouted. Miss Jo laughed and held his hand. "Eat up, Wesley. You have two more."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Sienna sat in the car. Her brown bear was gone. "Oh no," she said. "I can't find Bear!"

Daddy was in the driver's seat. "Where did you see Bear last?" he asked.

"I had Bear at home," said Sienna. "I hugged Bear in the house." She thought hard. "Then I got in the car. Bear was in my hand!"

Daddy smiled. "Then Bear is still close by. Things don't jump far. Look near your seat."

Sienna looked down. She looked under her legs. No Bear. She bent over and peeked under the seat. It was dark in there. She could not see.

"There is a little lamp in the door," said Daddy. He clicked it on. A warm light glowed.

Sienna peeked again. There was Bear! Bear had slipped out of her hand. Bear had fallen down, under the seat. "I dropped Bear, so Bear went down there!" said Sienna.

She pulled Bear out and hugged him tight. She kissed his brown nose. "Thank you, Daddy," she said. "Thank you, little lamp."

Daddy drove home. Sienna held Bear all the way. "Now we look under the seat first," she said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Grandma's house smelled like fried potatoes. It was Hanukkah, and Thomas got to help light the menorah.

"Pick a candle," said Grandpa. Thomas picked the blue one. He put it in the very last slot. "We light the new candle first," said Grandpa. Thomas held the little helper candle. He touched it to his blue candle. The flame popped up bright.

Then Grandpa lit the other candles from his blue flame. One by one they glowed. Thomas watched. "The new candle helped all the rest!" he said. "It did," said Grandpa. "Yours started it."

After that they ate hot latkes. Thomas wished for more applesauce. "Too late," said Aunt Jo, holding up the empty bowl. "You ate it all, silly." Thomas laughed and licked his fork. Outside the window, snow fell on the quiet street.

"Same time tomorrow," said Grandpa. Thomas clapped his hands.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Stella looked out the window. The sky had been stormy all night. Now the backyard was white. No school today! It was a snow day.

Stella put on her boots. She ran outside. The snow was deep and soft. She touched it with her mittens. It was very cold. She made a big snowball. Then she had a silly idea. Her toy cow was inside, waiting on the porch. "Mr. Cow needs a snow hat," she said. She put the snowball on the cow's head. The cow wore a white hat. Stella laughed and laughed.

Then she wanted to keep the snowball forever. She carried it inside. She set it on the table. She went to find Dad. They came back with cocoa. The snowball was gone! There was only a wet puddle. "The house is warm," said Stella. "Warm makes snow melt." Dad nodded. Stella tipped the puddle out the door. "Bye bye, snow. Come back tonight!"

story: Theodore stood in the gym at school. He wanted to throw the beanbag into the hoop. The hoop lay flat on the floor. He threw hard. The beanbag hit the hoop and bounced out. It landed in the hoop and stayed. "I threw soft, so it stayed in!" said Theodore. Next Miss Dot rolled him the big ball. He used one hand. The ball spun past his fingers. He tried both hands. The ball came right into them. "Both hands catch the big ball!" he said. Then they sat and ate crunchy crackers together.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Chloe went to the store with Dad. She wanted to buy a green apple for Grandma. Green was Grandma's favorite color.

Chloe looked in the fruit bin. She saw red apples. She saw yellow apples. But no green apples. Chloe felt sad. Then she saw a big sign. It said "Paint Sale." Buckets of paint sat on a shelf. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint.

Chloe had an idea. She picked up a brush. She dipped it in yellow paint. Then she dipped it in blue paint. She painted a paper apple. The apple turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," said Chloe. A store man smiled and gave her a green pig toy. It swung on a string. Chloe put the toy in the basket. It made the basket heavy, so Dad carried it.

At home, Grandma bit a yellow apple. She held the green painting up high. "My favorite," she said.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Nathan went to the park with Dad. There was a little fish stand by the pond. Nathan picked one small goldfish. "My first pet!" he said. He held the bag tight so it would not slip.

At home, Nathan gave the fish lots and lots of food. The next morning, the water looked cloudy. "Oh no," said Nathan. The fish swam slowly near the top. Nathan helped Dad clean the bowl. They put in fresh, clear water. Dad said to feed just one small pinch. Nathan gave one pinch, no more.

The next day, the water stayed clear. "Too much food made the water dirty," said Nathan. "Now I know." The goldfish swam fast and happy in its clean, shiny bowl. "Good morning, baby fish," said Nathan.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Charles ran to the little table. Today he would write his name! He picked up a pencil. He held it near the top, like a stick. The pencil slipped. His letter C came out wobbly and small.

His teacher sat next to him. She showed him her own hand. She held the pencil low, near the tip. Her fingers were snug and cozy, like a foot in a shoe. Charles tried it. He pinched the pencil near the point. He drew a big C. Then an H. Then A, R, L, E, S.

"Look!" he shouted. "I wrote Charles!" The letters stood in a row on the paper. He jumped up and waved it high. "I'm writing it again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Elijah got a small kitten from the vet. Her name was Pip. At home, Pip ran under the couch. She would not come out. Elijah peeked under. "Why are you hiding?" he asked.

He waited and watched. Maybe she was scared? The house was big and new to her. So Elijah sat very still. He put out a little food. He talked soft and slow. "It's okay, Pip."

Soon a small paw came out. Then Pip came out too. She ate the food. Her tummy got round. "You were scared because everything was new," Elijah said. "Now you know me."

The next day Pip was not grumpy anymore. She walked right up to Elijah. "Do you want to play?" he asked. Pip purred very loud.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rosalie sat at Grandma's house. It was Hanukkah. Daddy called everyone to the table.

Grandma lit the candles. "One, two, three, four," Rosalie counted. The flames were little and bright. "I want to blow them out," said Rosalie. "Like my birthday!" Grandma shook her head. "No, we watch them. We let them burn."

Rosalie waited. The candles got shorter and shorter. Where did the wax go? Did the fire eat it? Then one flame went out by itself. Pop, it was gone. Then another one. Soon all the candles were dark, all on their own.

"They went out!" said Rosalie. "Why, Grandma?" "They are short candles," said Grandma. "They burn down, and then the light is done." Rosalie spun her dreidel. It went round and round like a wheel. "I did not have to blow," she said. "The little candles did it themselves."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Austin went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big orange carrot on the shelf. It looked like a magic wand from his storybook. Austin reached up high on his toes. His fingers touched the shelf. Then his hand bumped a bag of frozen peas. The bag fell down with a thump. Peas rolled all over the floor like little green marbles.

"Sorry," said Austin to the peas. A store lady came to help. "Can you help us, please?" asked Mama. The lady smiled and picked up the bag. Austin helped too. He put the peas back one by one.

Then Austin held his carrot up like a wand. "Zap!" he said. The lady laughed. "Thank you," said Austin to her. "Thank you for helping."

At home, Mama cooked the carrot. Austin took a bite. It was sweet. "The peas fell because I bumped them," said Austin. "And the lady helped because we asked!" Mama kissed his head. Austin waved his carrot wand one more time. "Zap!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
It was a stormy night outside. Rain tapped on the window. Inside, it was warm and bright. Tonight Madeline's family would light the Hanukkah candles.

Papa put the menorah on the table. Madeline held the little candles in her hand. "I want to light them," she said. "You can hold the helper candle," said Papa. "It is called the shamash." The shamash was the tallest candle. It stood up higher than all the rest.

Madeline touched the shamash to a small candle. The small candle began to glow. Then the flame jumped to the next candle, and the next. "The tall candle lit them all," Madeline said. "One candle can share its fire." Grandma smiled. She gave Madeline a warm pancake. Madeline took a big bite and counted the lights. Outside, the storm kept on. Inside, eight little flames danced.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Mia was thirsty. She wanted cold water from the fridge. But her cup was up on the big shelf.

"Too big for me," she said. She looked around the kitchen. She found a small stool. The small stool made her tall. She reached and reached. Then she got her cup down. "One cup," she said. "Two hands. Three steps back."

She filled her cup at the sink. The water ran fast. It splashed and jumped. "Fast water makes a mess," said Mia. So she turned the tap a little. Now the water ran slow. Slow water filled the cup, drip by drip.

Her mama was making soup. The pot was hot. Mia saw steam rise up. She did not touch it. The fridge was cold. Her water was cold too.

"Why is the water cold, Mama?" she asked.
"Because it lived in the fridge," said Mama.

Mia took a big sip. Then a small sip. She put her cup down on the table, and the table had one wet ring on it.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Scarlett loved art time at school. Today she wanted to paint a frog. But there was no green paint on the tray. "Where is green?" she asked her teacher. "Look at the paint cups and see," said Ms. Lee.

Scarlett looked. She saw red paint. She saw yellow paint. She saw blue paint. No green anywhere. She patted the tray with her hand. It felt cool and smooth. She sniffed the cups. They smelled like paint, not like green.

Her friend Tomo sat next to her. He was painting a red fire truck. "I want green for my frog," Scarlett said. Tomo dipped his brush in yellow. Then he dipped it in blue. He made a mark on his paper. The mark turned green!

Scarlett opened her eyes wide. "Yellow and blue make green!" she said. She dipped her brush in yellow. She dipped it in blue too. She made a big wet dot. The dot was green, just like Tomo's. She had found out how to make her favorite color.

She painted her frog. It was green all over. She painted a green leaf next to it. Then she made a sign for her picture. She wrote her name on it in red. Ms. Lee hung the frog on the wall. "Look at my green frog!" Scarlett said. Tomo clapped for her.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Zoe rode in the car with Dad. The road was long. The sky was cloudy. They were going to the hospital. Mama was there with a new baby.

Zoe held her soft bear. She let the bear hide under her coat. "Shh," she said. "The baby is little."

They found Mama's room. Mama held a tiny baby. He had small hands and small feet. "This is Ben," said Mama. "He is your brother."

Then Ben began to cry. He cried and cried. Zoe felt sad. "Why is he sad?" she asked.

"Listen," said Mama. "He is hungry. Babies cry when they need something." Mama fed Ben some milk. He stopped crying. He made small sounds.

Zoe looked at Ben. "He cries because he is hungry," she said. "Now he is happy."

Later Ben cried again. Zoe said, "He needs something!" Mama picked him up. Ben hid his face in Mama's neck. Then he went to sleep.

Zoe patted his back, soft and slow. "Night night, Ben," she whispered.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Elena sat on her bed. The curtain moved. The wind made it go puff, puff. It was windy outside today.

The curtain went flap, flap, fast. Elena felt scared. She pulled the blanket up. Then she saw the tree by the window. The wind was moving the tree. The tree moved the curtain. She peeked out. "The wind did it," she said. She was not scared now.

Eena wanted to play. She sent her paper boat across the rug. "Boat, go to the pond," she said. The blue rug was the pond. The boat slid and stopped. Then it fell over. Elena felt angry. She stamped her foot.

She took a big breath, slow and long. Her body felt calm. She tried again, gently. This time the boat slid all the way. It sat on the blue pond. "You did it!" said Elena. She jumped up and down. Her teddy fell off the bed with a soft thump. Elena hugged him tight. "We are happy," she said. The curtain went puff, puff, slow now. Elena yawned. She sent the boat one more time, very softly, and closed her eyes.

story: Mason was at Grandma's house. Grandma gave him a big pencil and paper. "Write your name," she said. Mason grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. The pencil slipped. His M looked like a squiggly worm. Grandma laughed. "Try pinching it like a crab," she said. "Nip, nip!" Mason pinched the pencil with two fingers. The pencil stopped slipping. "My fingers turn it now," Mason said. He turned the pencil to make a big M. Grandma's cat jumped on the table. "Are you afraid of my cat?" asked Grandma. "No, I like her," said Mason. "But is she afraid of my M?" "Look, she is sleeping," said Grandma. Mason wrote his name. M, A, S, O, N. He counted the letters. One, two, three, four, five. Mason held up the paper. "Five letters, Grandma! All mine!"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Owen got to the playground early. The sun was warm on his face. Only one other kid was there, a girl with red boots.

Owen wanted to go down the big slide. He climbed one step. Then he stopped. His tummy felt funny. His legs felt wobbly. He was scared. "Why is my tummy jumpy?" he asked himself. He puffed a slow breath out, like blowing out a candle. He climbed another step. He puffed again. The jumpy feeling got smaller and smaller. At the top, he sat down and slid. "Wee!" His tummy felt light now, in a good way. He was excited.

The girl in red boots was building a sand tower. It fell down with a soft plop. Her lip wobbled. She was sad. Owen sat by her on the sand, which was soft like a pillow. They built the tower again, one handful at a time. It stood up tall. The girl laughed. Owen clapped his hands. "You did it!" he said. "Our tower is tall because we built it slow," said the girl. Owen slid down the big slide one more time, all by himself.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Matteo stood at the edge of the pool. The water looked big and blue. "I want to swim," he said. Mom held his hands in the water. Matteo's legs hung down. He did not move at all. "Kick your legs," Mom said. Matteo kicked. Splash, splash, splash! His legs made white bubbles. Now he moved! He moved all the way to the red ball. "I moved because I kicked," he said.

Mom let go of one hand. Matteo kicked again. Splash, splash, splash! He moved faster now. "Look at me!" he did shout to Dad. Dad laughed and clapped. Then Matteo stopped kicking. His legs went still. He stopped moving, too. The water held him like a thick blanket, but he did not go anywhere. He began to sink down a little. Mom lifted him up. "Kick again," she said softly. Matteo kicked. Up he came, and off he went. Splash, splash, splash!

A girl next to them was holding the wall. She looked scared. Her legs were still. "Kick your legs," Matteo said to her. "Then you move." The girl kicked. She moved! "I can swim!" she shouted. Matteo smiled a big smile. He turned and kicked toward the red ball again. Splash, splash, splash! "Wait for me!" he called to the ball.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Layla woke up in her big girl bed. "I am awake!" she said. Her tummy made a little growl. She ran to find Mama.

"Can I have toast?" she asked. Mama laughed. "Toast first, then we play." Layla ate her toast. She ate it all up, even the crust.

Then Layla saw snow out the window. "Snow! I want snow!" She grabbed her boots. She pushed her bare feet in. The boots would not go on. She pushed and pushed. Her toes said no.

Mama sat down next to her. "Try something else," said Mama. Layla looked at her feet. She looked at her socks on the floor. She put a sock on one foot. The sock made her foot small and smooth. The boot slid right on!

"Socks first, boots second," said Layla. "The sock makes my foot slippery!" Mama giggled. "You found it out all by yourself." Layla put on the other sock. She put on the other boot. She stomped like a bear.

Outside, the snow was cold and soft. Layla's heart felt like a drum. "Mama!" she called. "Look at me! I got dressed!" She made one big stomp in the snow. Her boot left a bear print.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Evan wanted the big yellow truck. It had a digger on the front. It could dig deep, deep holes.

But Sam had the truck. Sam was digging in the sand. Evan grabbed the truck. Sam held on tight. The truck did not move.

Teacher Mia came over. She held up one hand. "One more minute, Sam. Then it is Evan's turn," she said. Sam dug one more hole. Then he gave Evan the truck.

Evan dug a big hole. He looked at Sam. Sam looked sad. Evan gave the truck back. "Your turn," said Evan.

Sam smiled. He dug and dug. Then he gave the truck to Evan again. Back and forth it went. Evan thought about that. Did the truck feel bigger when they shared it? It looked like more truck somehow. Two boys, one truck, and so many holes in the sand.

At clean-up time, the bell rang. Everyone put the toys in the red box. Evan put the truck in last. The lid closed with a click.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Wyatt wanted a cup of water at school. Miss Kim had a big jug. "The water is cold," she said. Wyatt put his hand near it. Brrr, it was cold!

At snack time, Wyatt got hot cocoa in a big cup. He blew on it. He waited. It stayed hot. He waited more. Still hot. Wyatt had a want: he wanted to drink it now.

Then Wyatt saw a little cup on the shelf. He poured some cocoa into the little cup. The little cup was small. He blew once. He took a tiny sip. It was not too hot! The small cup made the cocoa cool fast. The big cup cooled slow.

Wyatt smiled. "Small cup, fast cool," he said. His friend Mia had a big cup too. Her face looked sad. "Too hot," she said. Wyatt poured her a little cup too. Mia blew once and drank it all. "Yum," she said. "Thank you, Wyatt." Then they went to build a tall tower of blocks.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Alice wanted to make pancakes. She wanted to make them all by herself.

First, Dad helped her wash her hands. Then she got to bathe the blueberries in a bowl of water. The little berries splashed and bobbed. "Clean berries, clean berries," she sang.

Alice poured the batter. Dad poured a square of butter into the pan. The butter went sizzle, sizzle. Then Alice dropped a big spoon of batter into the pan.

She waited. She waited. Nothing happened. "Why is it still runny?" she asked. Dad tapped the pan handle. "Look at the top," he said. Little bubbles popped up, pop, pop, pop. "The bubbles say it is ready," said Dad. Alice flipped the pancake. It turned golden brown. The first pancake was hers.

Then the dog ran in. He sat by the stove and licked his lips. Alice laughed. "No pancakes for dogs," she said. The dog put his paw on her slipper and did not move.

"Fine," said Alice. "One blueberry." The dog ate it in one gulp.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Nathan held his black teddy bear. His brother Sam held the tickets. The whole family was going on a trip, far from home.

"Wave one, wave two, wave three," said Nathan. The ferry went up and down. The waves made the boat rock. "The big wave pushed us," said Nathan.

Then Nathan went outside with Dad. The wind was strong. It blew Nathan's hat right off his head. "The boat goes fast, so the wind comes," said Nathan. Dad nodded and held Nathan's hand tight.

A seagull flew by. It landed on the rail near Sam. Sam had a biscuit in his hand. The seagull wanted it.

"Look out," said Nathan. Sam shared a little piece. The seagull ate it fast.

That night, Nathan dreamed about the big waves and the little white bird.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leon wanted to feed his teddy bear breakfast. He looked in the toy box. The toy box had cars and blocks and balls. "Those are toys," said Leon. "Teddy can't eat toys."

So Leon followed his mom to the kitchen. The kitchen had a fruit bowl. It held a fresh banana and a red apple. "Teddy can eat food," said Leon. "Fruit is food!"

Then Leon heard a bark at the door. It was his dog, Biscuit. Biscuit did not eat fruit. Biscuit ate food from his own bowl. Leon put dog food in Biscuit's bowl.

But wait. Teddy was gone! Leon looked under the table. There sat Biscuit, and on his back rode teddy, like a cowboy on a horse.

"Woof!" said Biscuit. "Giddy up!" said Leon. "The bear rides the dog!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Lea sat on the city bus with her mama. She held a new library card in her hand. She held a big red book, too. It was a book about a cat.

On the way home, Lea hugged the book. "This book is mine now," she said. "I want to keep it forever."

"You can keep it for a while," said Mama. "But we take it back on Friday. Then other kids can read it too."

Lea felt sad. She did not want to give the cat book back.

On Friday, they rode the bus again. Snowy windows made everything white outside. Lea put the book in the return box. It slid down with a soft thump.

Then a small girl ran up. She took the cat book off the shelf. She smiled big.

"That girl has the book because I brought it back," said Lea.

"Yes," said Mama. "And we can borrow it again."

Lea picked a new book. She sat close to Mama on the bus. "Let's read it at home," she said.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Rose wanted her red crayon. It was not in the box. "Where did it go?" she said.

Rose looked with her eyes. She saw the cat, the rug, and the table. No crayon. Then she heard a little sound with her ears. Tap, tap. It came from under the sofa. Rose got down on her knees. She touched the soft rug with her hands. She smelled something sweet near the sofa. It smelled like apples.

"Mom, come here!" said Rose. Mom lifted the sofa cover. There was the red crayon next to an old apple. "The apple rolled here," said Rose. "That is why my crayon hid!"

Rose licked her lips and smiled. "I found it with my eyes and my ears and my hands and my nose." She sat by the window and began to color. Outside the sky was cloudy, but her picture was all red.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Felix went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about a black cat. He could not find one.

Felix looked on a shelf. He saw books about cows. He saw books about pigs. "Those are animals," he said. He kept looking. He saw books about trucks and balls. "Those are toys," he said. He saw books about apples and bread. "Those are foods," he said.

A girl named Mia was there too. She dropped her books. Felix helped her pick them up. "Thank you," said Mia. She held up a book. It had a black cat on the front.

"That is my cat book," said Felix. "Can you show me where you found it?"

"It was with the animal books," said Mia. She put her head next to the cow books. "Cats and cows live together there."

Felix found the cat shelf. The cat book was big. He sat down with mama. Mama read it to him. Felix patted the black cat on the page. "Home now," he said. "Cats go with animals."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Charlie ran into the backyard. He held a small box. Inside was his very first pet. A bunny named Flop!

Charlie set the box down. Flop hopped out. Flop sniffed the grass. Then Flop began to chew it.

"Mom, come see!" Charlie called. Mom came fast. She smiled at Flop.

"Thirsty bunnies need water," Mom said. "Can you fill this bowl?"

Charlie filled the bowl at the tap. He set it by the grass. Flop hopped over. Flop drank and drank.

Charlie clapped his hands. "Flop drinks because I filled the bowl!" he said.

Mom held up her phone. "Smile!" she said. Click! The phone took a picture.

Now the yard had a fence, too. "The fence keeps Flop safe," said Mom.

Flop munched a green leaf. Charlie sat down close. He watched his bunny eat. "Good boy, Flop," Charlie whispered. "Tomorrow I will fill your bowl again."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Hunter wanted to help Dad in the backyard. Dad was cooking on the grill. Hunter stood next to Dad, like a big boy. "I stay close to you," Hunter said. Dad smiled.

The grill was hot. Hunter put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot!" he said, and pulled his hand back fast. Dad gave him a block of ice from the cooler instead. "Cold," Hunter said. He held the ice in his little hand. The ice felt good and smooth. A drop fell on his shoe and made a messy wet spot.

Hunter saw a stick on the ground. It was long and pointy. He did not touch it. "Pointy sticks can poke," he said. Then he smelled the hot dogs cooking. Dad put one on Hunter's plate. Hunter sat on the step and took a big bite. "The grill was hot because of the fire," Hunter said. Dad laughed. "That's right, big helper."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Sienna had to get a shot today. She waited in a small room with her mom. "Will it hurt?" Sienna asked. "Just a quick pinch," Mom said. "I will hold your hand."

The nurse came in with a tiny bandage. Sienna made her arm very stiff. She held it tight like a brick. The nurse said, "Let your arm go soft, like a noodle." Sienna let it flop down. The nurse wiped her arm with a cool cotton ball. Then the shot came. It was one small pinch, and it was done. "My soft arm made it quick," Sienna said. "Tight makes it slow. Soft makes it fast."

The sky outside looked stormy. But inside the ice cream shop it was warm. Sienna picked pink ice cream with a flower made of candy on top. Mom took a big lick of hers. "My arm is all better," Sienna said. She waved her sticker at the lady behind the counter.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Leo ran to the play corner at school. Today it was a pretend house! There was a little stove and a small bed. On the bed sat a baby doll. The doll was crying. "Waa, waa," said Mia, making the doll's voice. "The baby is hungry!"

"Baby needs a bottle," said Mia. But there was no bottle anywhere. Leo looked in the box. One pot, two cups, three spoons, no bottle. Leo wanted to help so much. Then he saw a yellow block. The block was long like a bottle. He held it to the doll's mouth. "Here, baby, drink," he said.

The doll got quiet. "The baby thinks the block is a bottle!" said Leo. Mia clapped her hands. "You fed her!" she said. "Now it is my turn," said Mia. She took the block and patted the doll's back. One pat, two pats, three pats. The baby went to sleep in the small bed.

Then Sam ran over. "Can I play?" he asked. "You can be the big sister," said Mia. "Big sisters help." Sam picked up the pot. He stirred one, two, three times. "Dinner is ready!" he said.

Leo smiled big. "The baby slept because I fed her," he said. "And the bottle was just a block!" He ran to get a cup. Maybe the cup could be a phone. He put it to his ear. "Ring, ring! Hello, this is Leo's house!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
James ran into writing club with a big smile. He wanted to write his name all by himself. His teacher, Miss Kim, gave him a fat pencil and some paper.

James grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The J came out all wobbly. The A looked like a little squiggle. "Oh no," said James. "My letters are messy."

Miss Kim sat next to him. "Try this," she said. She showed him how to pinch the pencil with two fingers. Thumb on one side. First finger on the other. The pencil sat on his middle finger like a little rest. James tried it. "It feels like I am holding a pet," he said. "Soft and gentle."

He pinched. He wrote a J. It popped right onto the paper, nice and straight! "Look!" said James. "The J is good!" He wrote A, then M, then E, then S. The A stood tall. The S curled just right. He was so excited that he jumped up.

"My paper is full of my name!" said James. "The letters are neat because I pinch, not squeeze!" Miss Kim clapped. James wrote his name one more time, slow and proud, and held the paper up high.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Kayden ran to the kitchen table. His lunch was there. A warm bun and a red apple.

"Mama, I want to eat now!" he said.

"Not yet," said Mama. "Your hands have germs on them. First we wash with soap. We wash for twenty seconds. Count with me."

Kayden stood at the sink. Mama put soap on his hands. He rubbed them together. Bubbles grew and grew.

They counted, "One, two, three..." all the way to twenty. The bubbles went down the fall of warm water. Splash, splash, gone.

Kayden looked at his hands. Were the germs gone too? He could not see germs. But Mama said twenty seconds was long enough to wash them away.

Mama gave him a dry towel. Kayden patted his hands. Then he held his apple. "My hands are clean now," he said.

He took a big, happy bite.

The next day, Kayden ran to the sink all by himself. "One, two, three..." he counted. He washed and washed. Twenty seconds, all done. Then he ran to the table for his snack.

"Did you use soap?" Mama asked.

"Yes! Twenty seconds," said Kayden. He held up his hands to show her. They were wet and shiny. Mama smiled and gave him the dry towel.

Kayden planted a big kiss on his clean hand. "Bye bye, germs," he said.
